name: Gandhism
info: Gandhism, also called Gandhianism, is the body of ideas drawn from the life and work of Mohandas K. Gandhi, built on truth and nonviolence; it shaped India's independence movement and later civil resistance movements elsewhere.

facts.thinkers: Mohandas K. Gandhi, whose life and work the ideas are drawn from; Henry David Thoreau, Leo Tolstoy and John Ruskin among his Western sources; Raychandbhai Mehta, the Jain guru near his home; Vinoba Bhave, who used the term sarvodaya for the post-independence struggle; Jawaharlal Nehru, whom Gandhi named his successor in 1942
facts.texts: Gandhi's autobiography, The Story of My Experiments with Truth; Thoreau's Civil Disobedience (1849); Tolstoy's The Kingdom of God Is Within You (1894); Ruskin's Unto This Last (1862), which Gandhi translated into Gujarati as Sarvodaya in 1908; Gandhi's articles in Indian Opinion and Harijan
facts.ideas: satya (truth); ahimsa (nonviolence); satyagraha, nonviolent resistance; fasting as mental control and penance; khadi, homespun cloth, and self-sufficiency; Gram Swaraj, decentralised village economies; sarvodaya, the uplift of all; the equal truth of all religions
facts.today: Sarvodaya groups descended from the networks of Vinoba Bhave still work locally in India; the journal Gandhi Marg has been published since 1957 by the Gandhi Peace Foundation; Gandhian methods are cited in civil rights and anti-apartheid movements and in democracy movements in Poland and Myanmar

t: Gandhi did not approve of the term Gandhism and said he had originated no new doctrine; the ideas are therefore derived by others from his life and works, and one such reading rests on truth and nonviolence.

Satyagraha, the nonviolent resistance he developed, drew on Thoreau's Civil Disobedience, Tolstoy, Ruskin and Indian religious thought, and was later taken up by Martin Luther King Jr., Nelson Mandela, Lech Wałęsa and Aung San Suu Kyi.

Gandhians disagreed with one another and with their critics: Gandhi's 1918 appeals to Indians to enlist in the First World War raised doubts among his own supporters, and Jinnah and Savarkar both condemned him over partition, from opposite sides.
dyk: In 1907 Gandhi called Thoreau's logic "incisive" and "unanswerable" in Indian Opinion, and he adopted from Thoreau's essay both the name civil disobedience and the means of breaking laws in order to call for their reform.
ev: Thoreau's name first appears in Indian Opinion, the journal Gandhi was editing in South Africa
Gandhi coins the word sarvodaya as the title of his translation of Ruskin's Unto This Last
Gandhi issues two public appeals for Indians to enlist in the British Indian Army in the First World War
Gandhi and his supporters march from Ahmedabad to Dandi in Gujarat in defiance of the salt monopoly
Gandhi fasts against separate electorates for Untouchable Hindus, and the Poona Pact with B. R. Ambedkar follows
The Quit India Movement opens civil resistance against British rule
A committee to promote Gandhi's teaching is formed, and the Gandhi Peace Foundation begins publishing Gandhi Marg

sections.origins:
Gandhism is a body of ideas that describes the inspiration, vision and life work of Mohandas K. Gandhi, particularly his contribution to nonviolent resistance. Gandhi did not approve of the term. He said there was no such thing as Gandhism, that he did not want to leave any sect after him, and that he had simply tried to apply eternal truths to daily life and problems. Because no Gandhism approved by Gandhi exists, one school of thought holds that it has to be derived from his life and works.

His thought has several earlier influences. In London he came under the influence of Henry Stephens Salt, whose A Plea for Vegetarianism turned him to the question of food and brought him to the vegetarian societies, where he found a cause and his first English friends. Thoreau's essay Civil Disobedience of 1849 was of greater importance than Walden: Gandhi was already conducting a form of civil disobedience in South Africa when he read it, and took from it the name and the means of breaking laws to call for their reform. Leo Tolstoy's critique of institutional Christianity moved him, and he named his settlement Tolstoy Farm. Ruskin's Unto This Last, given to him by Henry Polak, was a source of Gram Swaraj, his decentralised and self-sufficient economy. His first exploration of pluralism began with the Jain guru Raychandbhai Mehta.
sections.ideas:
The pivotal element of Gandhism is satya, truth, a virtue of being truthful in thought, speech and action. One deduction from Gandhi's life and works takes two principles: first, accepting the truth that people differ at every level, and second, never resorting to violence to settle those differences, whether between two people, two nations, two races or two religions. Satyagraha joins the Sanskrit words satya and agraha, to seek or desire, and became widely known during the Indian Independence Movement. Gandhi set out his philosophy in his autobiography, The Story of My Experiments with Truth.

Nonviolence, ahimsa, has a long history in Indian religious thought. Gandhi wrote that there were causes he was prepared to die for but none he was prepared to kill for. In a letter of July 1918 he nevertheless held that a conception of nonviolence that forbade self-defence was erroneous, and by 1924 he admitted that he lacked the strength of heart to follow the example of Swaminarayan, whom he now admired. He held that fasting brought the body under the mind's control and could cleanse the spirit, and he undertook fasts unto death on three notable occasions. On religion he described his beliefs as rooted in Hinduism and the Bhagavad Gita, held that all religions contain truth and some error, and believed that truth, ahimsa and the Golden Rule lay at the core of every religion.
sections.spread:
In his economics Gandhi favoured simple living and self-sufficiency, with import substitution rather than exports, and pictured a more agrarian India that would meet its people's material needs before it generated wealth or industrialised. His adoption of khadi, homespun cloth, was meant to help end poverty and social and economic discrimination and was a protest against colonial economic policy. He urged members of the Indian National Congress to spend time each day at the charkha, the spinning wheel, partly to link privileged Brahmins and lawyers in Congress with the peasantry, and Motilal Nehru and others gave up Western dress for it. The Khadi movement formed part of the larger swadeshi movement.

The word sarvodaya, universal uplift, was coined by Gandhi in 1908 as the title of his translation of Ruskin's Unto This Last. After independence Vinoba Bhave used it for the struggle of Gandhians to bring self-determination and equality to the masses. Bhave's associates, including Jaya Prakash Narayan and Dada Dharmadhikari, ran projects of popular self-organisation in the 1950s and 1960s. Gandhians have come from several faiths: Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the "Frontier Gandhi", who organised the Pathans of the Northwest Frontier as early as 1919; the Briton Horace Alexander; Martin Luther King Jr.; Hermann Kallenbach; and the atheist Jawaharlal Nehru.
sections.power:
Gandhi was assassinated in 1948, and his teachings are held to have played a major role in India's economic and social development and foreign relations for decades. On 15 January 1942 he openly proclaimed Jawaharlal Nehru his successor. Nehru was not religious and often disagreed with Gandhi, but he was deeply influenced by him and used his premiership for policies based on Gandhi's principles. His foreign policy was anti-colonial and neutral in the Cold War, and he helped found the Non-Aligned Movement. He also pushed through legislation granting legal rights to Indian women and outlawing untouchability, against strong opposition from orthodox Hindus.

Nehru was not Gandhian in several respects. He refused to condemn the Soviet invasion of Hungary in 1956–57, followed a socialist economic model unlike Gandhi's, and brought Goa and Hyderabad into the Indian union through military invasion. Some of his economic policies were criticised for removing the property rights of the landowning peasants of Gujarat for whom Gandhi had fought in the early 1920s. Gandhi himself believed in a kind of socialism very different from Nehru's, and called the difference one of emphasis, his on means and Nehru's on ends. Nehru's two biggest failures are thought to be the partition of India and the Sino-Indian War of 1962, in which his policy is said to have been influenced by Gandhian pacifism.
sections.critiques:
Gandhi's rigid ahimsa implies pacifism and is a source of criticism from across the political spectrum. On partition he wrote in Harijan in October 1946 that the demand for Pakistan was un-Islamic and sinful, yet he also proposed an agreement under which Congress and the Muslim League would cooperate to win independence, after which a plebiscite in Muslim-majority districts would decide partition. This double position exposed him to attack from both sides. Muhammad Ali Jinnah and his contemporaries condemned him for undermining Muslim political rights. Vinayak Damodar Savarkar and his allies accused him of appeasing Muslims while overlooking their atrocities against Hindus and of allowing the creation of Pakistan.

Many Indians condemned his refusal to protest against the executions of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, Udham Singh and Rajguru by the colonial government. Economists such as Jagdish Bhagwati have criticised his ideas of swadeshi. His 1932 fast against separate electorates for Untouchable Hindus brought controversy and conflict with B. R. Ambedkar; both made concessions in the Poona Pact, which dropped separate electorates in return for voluntary representation and a commitment to abolish untouchability. In July 1940 Gandhi appealed to Britons to meet Nazism with nonviolence, even at the cost of being slaughtered, and later he answered critics who said nonviolence could not stop Hindu–Muslim riots and that people should arm themselves.
sections.legacy:
Gandhi's commitment to nonviolent civil disobedience is credited with inspiring Martin Luther King Jr., Julius Nyerere, Nelson Mandela, Steve Biko, Lech Wałęsa and Aung San Suu Kyi. His work in South Africa between 1910 and 1915 for the rights of Indian residents is said to have inspired the African National Congress, which from the 1950s organised nonviolent civil disobedience akin to the Indian National Congress campaigns of the 1920s to 1940s. After the ANC won the first universal elections in 1994, Mandela visited India and honoured Gandhi as the man who inspired the freedom struggle of black South Africans. King travelled to India in 1962 to discuss Gandhi's teachings with Nehru, and the protests that followed are linked with the Civil Rights Act of 1964.

The nonviolent Solidarity movement in Poland overthrew a Soviet-backed communist government in 1989. In Myanmar, Aung San Suu Kyi was placed under house arrest and released in November 2010. In India a committee formed in 1957 to promote Gandhi's teaching recommended books and a Gandhi week for schools, and the Gandhi Peace Foundation has published the journal Gandhi Marg since 1957. A reading of his use of symbols holds that the Dandi March, the burning of British-made cloth and his fasts were means of spreading his ideas. Gandhi disliked having a cult following and was averse to being called Mahatma.

summary: Gandhism is the body of ideas drawn from Mohandas K. Gandhi's life and work, centred on truth and nonviolent resistance, though Gandhi himself rejected the term. It shaped India's independence movement and Nehru's policies, and inspired civil resistance movements in the United States, South Africa, Poland and Myanmar.
references: Mark Shepard, Gandhi Today: A Report on Mahatma Gandhi's Successors (Shepard Publications, 1987)
notes: Start 1908, circa true: the article gives no founding date for Gandhism and Gandhi rejected the term; 1908 is the year it gives for his coining of sarvodaya, and 1907 for Thoreau's name first appearing in Indian Opinion. Satyagraha's date is not given beyond 'popularised during the Indian Independence Movement'.
The dyk's 'In 1930 ... behind him' is awkward: the article gives 1907 for the Indian Opinion mention. Editor may reword; the 1907 fact and Thoreau's 1849 essay are the article's.

The article says of the 1930 Dandi March that the marchers disobeyed 'the Rowlatt Act which imposed taxes on salt production'; the Rowlatt Act is not a salt law in general knowledge, so I left the Act out and kept only the salt monopoly. It also says the 3 November 1930 speech was 'possibly one of Gandhi's last speeches' before the march; not used. No date for the march itself beyond 1930.

The article gives the 1922 fast as after Chauri Chaura, 1932 over the Communal Award, and 1947 for Bengal and Delhi, and also dates his last fast speech 1 December 1948, after his assassination in 1948; it is contradictory on that, so the 1948 fast is left out. 'Fast Unto Death' is the article's term for all three.
The Poona Pact event (1932) is described in the article as the outcome of Gandhi's fast and Ambedkar's concessions; the year of the pact is not given separately.
The article says the Quit India Movement was an 'offensive in civil resistance' in 1942; no month given. Gandhi's 1940 Harijan appeal (6 July 1940) is summarised in critiques only.

The article says Nehru's 'two biggest failures are thought to be' partition and the 1962 war and that his wartime policy 'is said to have been influenced by Gandhian pacifism'; both attributed with hedges. A final sentence on Nehru neglecting the defence budget is left out as unattributed.

The article credits King's protests with 'precipitating' the Civil Rights Act and Solidarity with 'precipitating the downfall of the Soviet Union'; I kept the first as the article's connection and left out the second. The article says Biko was 'allegedly murdered in 1977'; left out. The article's Suu Kyi paragraph dates the military's dismissal of elections to 1991; left out as it is probably 1990.
Sections 'power' and 'legacy' are the post-independence influence: the article names no state that applied Gandhism as a doctrine and gives no record of repression or famine, so none is told.

Left out: the sentence that Gandhi's 1918 advocacy 'of violence' and his remark about India's ascetic culture (kept only as the enlistment appeals and the letter's view on self-defence); the Swaminarayan sociologist N. A. Thoothi's claims; the propaganda reading by Lasswell beyond the symbols; Gandhi's remarks on his early life (hitting his wife, meat, cigarette); the Gandhi Marg editors and external links.
